EVADE / Weekly brief 001 / US equities

Strong growth.
Expensive capital.

The next test for US equities: can earnings and cash flow justify the investment being made today?

Draft · Founder review pendingWeek ending 30 October 2026Prepared 31 October

The question: strong quarterly demand and persistent inflation sit alongside softer monthly household spending. The equity test is how that mix reaches earnings, investment and cash flow.

The opening view

Resilient growth and persistent inflation leave equities sensitive to real interest rates and the cash returns on AI investment. The useful tension is between strong quarterly domestic demand and a weak September reading for real household spending. This supports selective company research; it does not establish that equities are generally mispriced.

The marginal variables for the coming week are labor-market resilience and real yields. For AI infrastructure, the separate question is whether capacity spending becomes durable cash flow per share. Confidence in this interpretation is moderate; confidence in a short-term equity direction is lower.

What the week established

Markets: AP reports Friday closes of 7,580.07 for the S&P 500 and 25,437.00 for the Nasdaq Composite, with weekly declines of 0.6% and 2.0%, respectively. These are price-index changes, not total returns. [1]

Growth: the advance estimate put Q3 real GDP growth at 3.4% annualized, versus 2.2% in Q2. Real final sales to private domestic purchasers grew 4.9%. Investment, including inventories and computer equipment, contributed to the acceleration. This is stronger evidence of demand than headline GDP alone, but an advance estimate remains revisable. [2]

Inflation and consumers: September headline PCE inflation was 3.6% year over year and core was 3.1%; the monthly increases were 0.5% and 0.3%. Real consumption rose less than 0.1%, real disposable income fell 0.3%, and the saving rate was 3.8%. The monthly picture is softer than the quarterly growth story. Q3 core PCE inflation of 2.5% annualized measures a different horizon and must not be confused with September's 3.1% year-over-year rate. [2] [3]

Policy: on 28 October the Fed held its target at 3.75%-4.00%. Two dissenters preferred a 25-basis-point increase. A hold therefore provides little support for assuming imminent easing. That last statement is our interpretation, not an estimate of futures-implied probabilities. [4]

Labor: the frozen current-vintage data show September unemployment at 4.2%, versus 4.1% in August; payrolls increased 29,000. Initial claims were 194,000 for the week ending 24 October. Low claims argue against an abrupt layoff wave, while weak hiring is meaningful contrary evidence. Neither alone settles the labor outlook. [5]

Rates and credit: the latest retrieved 10-year nominal and real yields are 4.98% and 2.63%, both dated 29 October. The high-yield option-adjusted spread was 3.26 percentage points that day, versus 3.38 on 23 October. These observations do not describe Friday's bond close and do not establish a broad credit shock. [6]

The company test: Microsoft

Our causal hypothesis: persistent inflation limits easing; sustained real yields raise the return demanded on distant cash flows; high investment requirements make funding quality and monetization more important. The contrary mechanism is equally concrete: strong demand and productivity can lift earnings sufficiently to offset the valuation pressure.

Microsoft provides a useful test. Its September quarter revenue was $92.3bn, up 19%, while Azure revenue grew 48%. The company reported $677bn in commercial remaining performance obligations. These support a demand case, but backlog is not immediate revenue or profit. [7]

Matched SEC cash-flow facts for 1 July-30 September show $58.000bn operating cash flow and $39.367bn cash PP&E purchases: $18.633bn cash FCF, or roughly 68% of operating cash flow consumed by cash capex. This calculation excludes finance-lease additions. It does not by itself measure total investment obligations, maintenance spending, incremental ROIC or sustainable owner earnings. [8]

Next company work: reconcile leases, working-capital benefits and customer prepayments; examine depreciation and capacity utilization; connect RPO conversion to margins and FCF per share. Until those checks and a dated valuation are complete, Microsoft is a research candidate, not a price-target call.

Geopolitics through cash flows

The EIA's 6 October outlook assumes Middle East oil flows remain constrained during Q4. Its assumptions were finalized on 1 October, so it is background evidence rather than a current security update. The equity mechanism to monitor is energy and freight costs feeding into consumer purchasing power, transport/industrial margins and inflation persistence. A verified improvement in physical flows would weaken this pressure. We have not verified a new geopolitical event this week and make no forecast about military outcomes. [9]

What would change the view?

Base case: growth holds up, inflation remains uncomfortable and real yields stay elevated; equity selection depends on earnings delivery and funding quality. Confirmation: labor stays broadly stable and real yields remain near current levels.

Equity upside: inflation pressure and real yields ease without a sharp growth deterioration; company cash conversion improves. A real-yield move below 2.50% would challenge our near-term rate view, although a recession-driven decline would not automatically be bullish for equities.

Equity downside: weakening employment and household demand meet persistent input costs; margins and earnings expectations deteriorate. Unemployment above 4.4% in October's initial release would challenge our labor-resilience forecast. Widening credit spreads would be a separate warning, not something inferred from stock prices.

Observed technology weakness is consistent with reassessment of long-duration earnings, but cannot identify the cause or prove an opportunity. Verified forward consensus, valuation spreads, options pricing and positioning are missing. Our relative-index call is consequently an exploratory hypothesis, not demonstrated alpha; Nasdaq versus S&P also mixes sector and size exposures.

The week ahead

3 November: US federal election; assess actual policy implications without assuming an outcome. September JOLTS at 16:00 Zagreb / 10:00 US Eastern.
5 November: preliminary Q3 productivity at 14:30 Zagreb / 08:30 US Eastern.
6 November: October employment at 14:30 Zagreb / 08:30 US Eastern.
These times account for the US return to standard time. Check the release calendars again before review. [10] [11]

How this brief was prepared

Independent, AI-assisted research using free public sources, informed by Stoic Research’s teaching. This is EVADE’s own analysis and forecast record. The supplied teaching files are not reproduced here.

Research was recorded on 31 October 2026 at 00:57 UTC. Market data carry their own observation dates: the rates shown end on 29 October; Friday equity closes come from AP. The automated index feeds had not yet caught up. Latest-vintage economic data are retained for prospective review, not presented as a historical backtest.

The brief is a US edition. It does not replace the planned US-and-Europe scorecard or substitute the Nasdaq Composite for the Nasdaq-100. Forward consensus, options pricing and positioning remain gaps in this analysis.

These are subjective forecasts with no resolved outcomes yet. The journal will assess reasoning quality separately from accuracy. Founder review remains pending.
